logline: A woman joins a drug cartel to avenge her father's murder, then infiltrates the police as a mole, only to find that her loyalties and her identity are impossible to separate.

bollymeter.basis: Han So-hee's physically committed performance and the show's lean, uncompromsing eight-episode shape make it the tightest Korean action noir of 2021; rare 100 percent Rotten Tomatoes score reflects critical unity.

pull_quotes.text: Han delivers a performance of great physicality, intensity and occasional vulnerability; My Name works on a range of levels.
A very different show worthy of just as much attention, delivering a handsome, engaging, bloodthirsty spectacle with plenty of style and verve.

seasons.review_body: My Name arrives quietly and builds momentum through word of mouth, eventually landing some of the strongest critical notices any Korean action drama on Netflix has earned. The pitch is tight: a bereaved daughter accepts gang membership in exchange for a shot at the man who killed her father, then operates undercover inside the police drug unit hunting her own boss. Director Kim Jin-min stages the hand-to-hand combat with unusual physicality, and Han So-hee trained extensively to perform it herself. The mid-section reads as the weaker stretch, where plot mechanics slow the emotional momentum, though the lead performance remains unchallenged and the eight-episode structure stays remarkably efficient. It starts slower than it ends, but the final three episodes close the loop with precision.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: On her birthday, Ji-woo watches her father die and commits immediately to the only plan that makes sense to her: gang membership, training, revenge. The episode compresses backstory and motivation with unusual economy, and Han So-hee's physicality is already visible in how Ji-woo holds herself after the opening scene.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Ji-woo arriving at the gang leader's door - the choice the rest of the series is built on, made in grief without hesitation.

critic_note.text: Han delivers a performance of great physicality, intensity and occasional vulnerability; My Name works on a range of levels.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 3
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Ji-woo is now undercover as a police officer and working alongside the detective hunting her own boss. The dramatic irony is sharp and the hand-to-hand action sequences - choreographed for Han So-hee's trained physicality rather than cinematic convention - begin establishing the show's tonal identity.
episode_reviews.the_moment: A raid scene where Ji-woo has to fight her way through people who think she is on their side.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 7
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The facts about Ji-woo's father's death arrive in a sequence that reframes everything she thought she understood about the show's central question, reshaping the earlier assumptions viewers carried into the story. The mid-section lag is where the series starts to regain momentum decisively, recalibrating the pace for what follows.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Ji-woo learning the truth about her father - a revelation the show was precise enough to earn and honest enough not to soften.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 8
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale closes Ji-woo's arc with a fight that is as much about identity as it is about survival. The revenge question is answered in a way that feels morally coherent rather than satisfying in the conventional genre sense - the show's most honest decision.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Ji-woo's final confrontation - the scene Han So-hee built the entire series toward.

critic_note.text: A very different show worthy of just as much attention, delivering a handsome, engaging, bloodthirsty spectacle with plenty of style and verve.
